title: "Code highlighting"
description: "How Quarto highlights code blocks and inline code with tree-sitter, which languages are built in, how to add a language by shipping a tree-sitter grammar (a `.wasm` file and `highlights.scm`) in `_quarto/grammars/`, how capture names become `hl-*` CSS classes, and how a Lua filter can supply highlighting itself."
---

## Overview

Quarto highlights code at render time with
[tree-sitter](https://tree-sitter.github.io/tree-sitter/) grammars. Give a
fenced code block a language and its contents are parsed and colored:

````markdown
```python
def greet(name):
    return f"Hello, {name}!"
```
````

Inline code works the same way, with the language as a class:
`` `len(xs)`{.python} ``.

When a code block or inline code has several classes, the **first class
that names a known language** chooses the grammar, so both
```` ```{.python .numberLines} ```` and ```` ```{.numberLines .python} ````
highlight as Python. A block with no recognized language is rendered as
plain code, without an error or warning.

Highlighting applies to the HTML-based formats (`html`, `revealjs`, and
dashboards). The colors come from the `syntax-highlighting:` palette; see
[Syntax highlighting](../formats/html/themes.qmd#syntax-highlighting) for
choosing a palette and for light and dark variants.

## Built-in languages

These languages need no setup. Each language name in the table works as a
code block class, and so does each alias.

| Language   | Aliases     |
|------------|-------------|
| bash       | `sh`        |
| css        |             |
| html       |             |
| javascript | `js`, `jsx` |
| json       |             |
| julia      | `jl`        |
| lmd        |             |
| lua        |             |
| python     | `py`        |
| r          |             |
| rust       | `rs`        |
| sql        |             |
| tsx        |             |
| typescript | `ts`        |
| yaml       | `yml`       |

## Adding a language with a tree-sitter grammar

To highlight a language that isn't built in, put a tree-sitter grammar in
your project. Quarto looks in `_quarto/grammars/`, and each subfolder there
holds one grammar:

```text
my-project/
├── _quarto.yml
├── document.qmd
└── _quarto/
    └── grammars/
        └── toml/
            ├── toml.wasm        # the grammar, compiled to WebAssembly
            └── highlights.scm   # the grammar's highlight query
```

No `_quarto.yml` setting is needed: every subfolder that contains both a
`.wasm` file and a `highlights.scm` file is loaded, and the language it
serves is the `.wasm` file's name without the extension. With the layout
above, ```` ```toml ```` blocks and `` `…`{.toml} `` inline code are
highlighted with the TOML grammar. For a single document that isn't part
of a project, `_quarto/grammars/` sits next to the document.

@demo-user-grammar shows a document highlighting TOML this way:

:::: {#demo-user-grammar .embed-example-iframe file="/examples/highlighting/01-user-grammar/document.html"}
````markdown
---
title: "A user-supplied grammar"
format: html
---

TOML is not one of Quarto's built-in highlighting languages. This
project adds it by shipping a tree-sitter grammar in
`_quarto/grammars/toml/`: the compiled `toml.wasm` and its
`highlights.scm` query. Any code block marked `toml` now picks it up:

```toml
# Site configuration
[server]
host = "localhost"
port = 8080
debug = false
started = 2026-11-05T09:30:00Z

[[server.routes]]
path = "/docs"
cache = { enabled = true, max-age = 3600 }
```

Inline code works the same way: `retries = 3`{.toml}.
````

### Getting the grammar files

Many tree-sitter grammars publish a compiled `tree-sitter-<language>.wasm`
with each GitHub release, for example
[tree-sitter-toml](https://github.com/tree-sitter-grammars/tree-sitter-toml/releases).
Download it and rename it to the class you want to write on your code
blocks (`tree-sitter-toml.wasm` becomes `toml.wasm`). Without a release
asset, build one from the grammar's repository with
`tree-sitter build --wasm`.

Take `highlights.scm` from the same repository, usually at
`queries/highlights.scm`, and from the same version as the `.wasm`. A query
written for a different version of the grammar can name node types the
grammar doesn't have, and then the grammar fails to load.

Quarto uses tree-sitter 0.26, which loads grammars generated with
tree-sitter language ABI versions 13 to 15.

### Rules and limits

- **One grammar per folder.** A folder with more than one `.wasm` file is
  skipped without a warning. The folder's own name doesn't matter; the
  `.wasm` file name does.
- **The file name is the language name.** User grammars have no aliases. To
  serve both `toml` and another class, use two folders.
- **A user grammar replaces a built-in one.** Quarto checks user grammars
  before its built-in grammars, so a `_quarto/grammars/python/python.wasm`
  takes over every `python` block. A user grammar named after a built-in
  alias, such as `py.wasm`, takes over only that alias.
- **Only `highlights.scm` is read.** `injections.scm` and `locals.scm` are
  ignored, so code embedded in another language (for example JavaScript
  inside HTML) is not highlighted by a user grammar.
- **Problems are warnings, not errors.** If a grammar fails to load, the
  render prints a `failed to load user grammars from …` warning and
  continues, and the affected blocks render unhighlighted. A `.wasm` named
  differently from the class on your code blocks produces no warning: the
  grammar loads, but nothing asks for it.
- **Previews load the same folder.** Live previews in `q2 preview` and
  Quarto Hub pick up `_quarto/grammars/` too, so a grammar added there
  highlights in the preview and in the rendered output alike.

## How capture names become CSS classes

A grammar's `highlights.scm` assigns **capture names** to parts of the
syntax tree. For example, this line from the TOML query marks every comment:

```scheme
(comment) @comment
```

Quarto wraps each captured piece of code in a `<span>` whose class is the
capture name with an `hl-` prefix and dots turned into hyphens. `@comment`
becomes `<span class="hl-comment">` and `@function.builtin` becomes
`<span class="hl-function-builtin">`. When captures nest, the innermost one
colors each character.

The palettes color the standard tree-sitter capture names: `attribute`,
`boolean`, `character`, `comment`, `constant`, `constructor`, `embedded`,
`error`, `escape`, `function`, `keyword`, `label`, `markup`, `module`,
`namespace`, `number`, `operator`, `property`, `punctuation`, `special`,
`string`, `tag`, `type` and `variable`, along with their common
refinements, such as `function.builtin`, `keyword.control` or
`string.special`. Most published `highlights.scm` files use these names.

A capture outside that set, such as `@string.special.key`, still produces a
span, but no palette colors it. Either change the capture in
`highlights.scm` to a standard name or style the class yourself in a
stylesheet:

```css
.hl-string-special-key {
  color: #8250df;
}
```

The same approach adjusts a standard capture. The full document behind
@demo-user-grammar ends with a rule that sets `.hl-type` (which the TOML query uses
for keys) in bold.

## Highlighting from a filter

A tree-sitter grammar isn't the only way to highlight a block. The
highlighter writes its result to a `data-hl-spans` attribute on the code
block, and if a block **already has** that attribute, Quarto leaves it
alone. A Lua filter can therefore highlight a block itself.

The value is a JSON array of `[start, end, capture]` triples. `start` and
`end` are byte offsets into the block's text, counted from 0, with `end`
exclusive. This filter marks the words `ERROR` and `WARN` in ```` ```log ````
blocks:

```lua
function CodeBlock(cb)
  if cb.attr.classes[1] ~= "log" then
    return nil
  end

  local spans = {}
  for _, row in ipairs({ { "ERROR", "error" }, { "WARN", "warning" } }) do
    local needle, capture = row[1], row[2]
    local init = 1
    while true do
      -- Plain find returns 1-based inclusive offsets; subtracting 1 from
      -- the start gives the 0-based, end-exclusive range.
      local s, e = cb.text:find(needle, init, true)
      if not s then break end
      table.insert(spans, { s - 1, e, capture })
      init = e + 1
    end
  end
  table.sort(spans, function(a, b) return a[1] < b[1] end)

  cb.attr.attributes["data-hl-spans"] = pandoc.json.encode(spans)
  return cb
end
```

The captures become classes exactly as grammar captures do (`error` becomes
`hl-error`, which the palettes color). `warning` is not a standard capture
name, so give `.hl-warning` a style of your own.
